summary: For ages 6–7, learners notice, describe and PREDICT repeating sky patterns from sustained first-hand observation: the Sun appears to rise on one side, arc across the sky and set on the other each day; the Moon changes shape over about a month; and stars are seen at night (but are still present, outshone, by day). Teaching stays firmly at describing and predicting patterns, deferring their causes to later topics. Core activities are a month-long Moon-shape diary, safely marking the Sun's position at morning/midday/afternoon by reading a shadow stick (never looking at the Sun), and a day-sky vs night-sky sort. A screen 'sky over time' scrubber and static phase/Sun-arc references are useful supports, and a short sequence/sort check can assess the pattern knowledge.
misconceptions: The Moon changes shape because clouds or something covers part of it, or it is a different Moon each night.
The Moon only appears at night — in fact it is often visible during the day.
Stars are not present in the daytime — they are there but outshone by the Sun.
The patterns of Sun, Moon and stars are random rather than predictable.
The Sun literally travels across the sky (recording the appearance is fine; the correct cause is deferred).

activities.title: Month-long Moon-shape diary
steps: Whenever the Moon can be seen in a clear sky (often in the evening, but on some nights it is not up at a child's evening viewing time or cannot be seen at all), draw the shape of the Moon you can see, dating each drawing, and mark 'not seen' on other nights.
Keep the drawings in order on a strip or class calendar so the sequence builds up over about a month.
After a week or two, look back at the pattern and PREDICT: draw what you think the Moon will look like in a few nights.
Check your prediction against the next real observation and talk about whether the shape is fattening or thinning.
Watch for and record any time you spot the Moon in the daytime too.
activities.insight: The Moon's shape changes in a dependable, repeating cycle over about a month, so you can use past observations to predict what comes next — and the Moon is sometimes visible by day, not only at night.

activities.title: Mark the Sun's daily path
steps: At morning, midday and afternoon on the same day, record where the Sun appears — safely and indirectly, by marking the shadow cast by a fixed stick or object (a shadow stick); the Sun is on the opposite side of the stick from its shadow. NEVER look at or stare directly at the Sun.

Compare the three recorded positions and describe the path: the Sun appears to climb higher towards midday (shortest shadow) and then get lower in the afternoon, fitting the pattern of rising on one side and setting on the other.
Predict where the Sun will appear at lunchtime (or another time), then check by reading the shadow again — not by looking at the Sun.
Sort a set of sky objects/pictures into 'seen by day', 'seen by night', and 'sometimes both' (Sun by day; stars by night; Moon sometimes in both).
activities.insight: The Sun follows the same daily rising-arcing-setting pattern (only shifting slowly over the seasons), so its apparent position at a given time is predictable; the Sun is seen by day and the stars by night, while the Moon can be seen in either.

activities.title: Dim-light predict-observe-explain (stars hidden by day)
steps: In a darkened room, turn on a small dim LED night-light.
Before anything changes, PREDICT with a reason: when all the big room lights come on, will the little light still be shining or will it go off? Commit to your answer out loud.
Turn on all the big lights and watch — the little light becomes much harder to see and may seem to vanish, even though it is still on.
Dim the room again and watch it reappear.
Say what this shows about why we can't see the stars in the daytime.
activities.insight: A dim light is still on even when a much brighter light washes it out — just as the stars are still present in the daytime but hidden by the bright, Sun-lit sky.

activities.title: Scrubbable 'sky over time' model (optional support)
steps: Drag a time slider forward: watch the Sun rise from one horizon, arc across the sky and set as the world darkens and stars appear.
Keep dragging across weeks and watch the Moon steadily fatten and thin through its shapes.
Before checking, predict: what will tonight's Moon look like, or where will the Sun be at lunchtime? Then drag to check.
Use a built-in Moon-diary capture that mirrors the shapes you have been recording in the real sky.
activities.insight: The sky's changes are a dependable, repeating pattern — not random — so advancing time lets you anticipate the next state, and the on-screen cycle lines up with your own real observations.

activities.title: Pattern check: sequence and sort
steps: Put a scrambled set of Moon-phase pictures back into the correct order.
Given the last few Moon shapes in order, choose which shape comes next.
Sort sky objects into day-sky vs night-sky (with 'sometimes both' available for the Moon).
Answer and give a reason: in the daytime, can you see the stars? Why do you think that is?
activities.insight: Demonstrate that you can describe and predict the sky patterns and explain that daytime stars are hidden, not gone.

checkQuestion: In the daytime, can you see the stars in the sky? … Now tell me why you think that is.
checkAnswer: You can't see the stars in the daytime because the sky is too bright — the Sun's light washes them out — but the stars are still there all along.
